node.title: Cytochrome c structure and role
node.canonical_question: What does cytochrome c do in the electron transport chain?
node.summary: Cytochrome c is a small mobile electron carrier. It shuttles electrons from Complex III to Complex IV.

render.heading: What cytochrome c does in the respiratory chain
render.body:
Cytochrome c is a small protein that acts as a mobile electron carrier in the electron transport chain.

Its job is to shuttle electrons between two large protein complexes embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane:

1. It picks up electrons from Complex III (also called the cytochrome bc1 complex). Complex III accepts electrons from ubiquinol (the reduced form of coenzyme Q) and transfers them one at a time to cytochrome c.

2. It carries those electrons across the intermembrane space and delivers them to Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase).

3. Complex IV collects four electrons from four cytochrome c molecules and passes them to one molecule of oxygen, reducing it to two molecules of water.

Why a mobile carrier is needed:

Complexes III and IV are large, rigid structures fixed in the membrane. They cannot reach each other directly. Cytochrome c is small and water-soluble enough to diffuse freely through the intermembrane space, so it bridges the gap between them.

The electron transfer is possible because cytochrome c contains a haem group — an iron-containing ring — whose iron atom cycles between the Fe2+ (reduced) and Fe3+ (oxidised) states as it accepts and donates electrons.

In summary, cytochrome c keeps electrons moving along the chain, ensuring that the final step — reduction of oxygen to water — can occur and that the proton gradient driving ATP synthesis is maintained.
